name: fsync
description: fsync() flushes all modified in-core data and metadata of the file referred to by the file descriptor to the storage device, ensuring data is retrievable after a system crash. It blocks until the transfer is complete. fdatasync() is similar but only flushes metadata necessary for subsequent data retrieval, reducing disk activity.

parameters.name: fd
parameters.description: File descriptor of the file to synchronize

return_value.failure: Returns -1 on error, and errno is set

errors.description: fd is not a valid open file descriptor
The function was interrupted by a signal
An error occurred during synchronization, possibly related to other file descriptors on the same file
Disk space was exhausted while synchronizing
fd is bound to a read-only filesystem
fd is bound to a special file (e.g., pipe, FIFO, or socket) which does not support synchronization
fd is bound to a file on a filesystem like NFS where a previous write failed due to insufficient storage space

bugs: In Linux 2.2 and earlier, fdatasync() is equivalent to fsync(), offering no performance advantage. Some older kernels and lesser-used filesystems do not properly flush disk caches, requiring manual disabling via tools like hdparm(8). Under AT&T UNIX System V Release 4, fd must be opened for writing, which is incompatible with POSIX but persists in some systems like HP-UX and AIX.
versions: POSIX.1-2001 and later; Linux 2.2 and above with specific behaviors for fdatasync()
